Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Specify the composition and function of tendons and ligaments.
Determine the biomechanical properties of tendons and ligaments, including their viscoelastic
behavior and the associated concepts of creep and stress relaxation.
Specify the differences in intra-articular and extra-articular tendons and ligaments with regard
to their observed healing properties.
Describe the process of ligamentization of anterior cruciate ligament grafts.
Describe the anatomic and structural differences between direct and indirect insertions of
tendons and ligaments at the enthesis.
Tendons
Anatomy and Function

Function: tendons transfer force from muscle to bone to produce joint motion and assist in
dynamic joint stabilization.
Composition and structure
Tendon is made up of densely packed collagen fibers and water, with trace amounts of
proteoglycans and elastin. The tissue is paucicellular.
Tendons may be classified by shape (round or flat), by anatomic location (intra-articular or
extra-articular), or by the surrounding layer of connective tissue (paratenon or synovium)1
(Resource 1).
The fibroblast is the predominant cell type in tendon.
Tendon has a hierarchical structure (Figure 1).
Type I collagen is the major constituent of tendon, contributing to approximately 86% of its
dry weight and 95% of matrix protein. The primary structure of collagen consists of glycine
(33%), proline (15%), and hydroxyproline (15%). The collagen molecule is fibrillar in structure,
with a length of 300 nm and a diameter of 1.5 nm.
Proteoglycans contribute to 1% to 5% of the dry weight of tendon.
Decorin is the predominant proteoglycan in tendon.
Aggrecan (a proteoglycan abundant in articular cartilage) is found in areas of tendon that are
under compression (eg, regions of hand flexor tendons that wrap around bone).
The vascularity of tendon varies. Sheathed tendons (eg, flexor tendons of the hand) have
regions that are relatively avascular. These regions get nutrition via diffusion from the
synovium. Tendons not enclosed by a sheath receive their blood supply from vessels
entering from the tendon surface or from the tendon enthesis (the tendon-to-bone insertion)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110

Figure 1 Illustration shows a tendon. Tendon has a hierarchical structure, with collagen
molecules assembled into progressively larger bundles, until the level of the tendon itself is
reached. Note the endotenon (surrounding the fascicle) and epitenon (surrounding the tendon),
containing the neurovasculature of the tendon. (Reproduced with permission from Counihan
MM, Soslowsky LJ: Tendons and ligaments, in Aaron R, ed: Orthopaedic Basic Science: Foundations
of Clinical Practice, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp
215-230.)

Anatomy and Function
Tendon is primarily composed of type I collagen, laid down by fibroblasts. In longitudinal
histologic sections, fibroblasts appear spindle-shaped, with a preferred orientation in the
direction of collagen fibers. In cross-section, fibroblasts are star-shaped, with long
cytoplasmic processes. The collagen structure of tendon is highly organized, with
collagen molecules arranged in quarter-stagger arrays. Five collagen molecules form an
ordered microfibril unit. Microfibrils combine to form subfibrils, which further combine
to form fibrils. Fibril units then form highly ordered parallel bundles oriented in the
direction of muscle force. Fibrils accumulate to form fascicle units, which then combine
to form the tendon. The role of decorin during development and healing is to regulate
collagen fiber diameter. The presence of decorin inhibits lateral fusion of collagen fibers.
The function of decorin in adult tendon is a subject of debate. Decorin molecules form
cross-links between collagen fibers. Studies have hypothesized that the molecules
transfer loads between collagen fibers, thereby increasing the stiffness of the tendon;
however, recent experimental evidence has disputed this hypothesis. Tendons with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
3/19

areas of relative avascularity include the supraspinatus tendon, long head of the biceps
tendon, Achilles tendon, and patellar tendon, all of which are prone to rupture.1
Biomechanics
Tendons are anisotropic; that is, mechanical properties vary based on the direction of loading.
They have high tensile properties and buckle under compression (ie, they behave similar to
ropes). A typical load-elongation curve for tendon includes a toe region, a linear region, and a
failure region (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Graph shows the tensile behavior of tendon and ligament tissue, which includes a
nonlinear toe region at low loads, a linear region at intermediate loads, and a failure region at
high loads. (Reproduced from Thomopoulos S: Tendons and ligaments, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 656-662.)
Tendon biomechanics can be characterized by structural properties (load-elongation behavior)
or material properties (stress-strain behavior, in which stress is calculated by dividing load by
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
4/19

cross-sectional area and strain is calculated by dividing change in elongation by initial length).
Tendons exhibit viscoelastic behavior; that is, the mechanical properties of the tissue depend
on loading history and time. Time dependence is best illustrated by the phenomena of creep
and stress relaxation.
Creep is the increase in strain over time for a constant applied stress. 
Stress relaxation is the decrease in stress over time for a constant applied strain.
Several factors influence the biomechanical properties of tendons:
Anatomic location
Exercise and immobilization
Patient age
The following factors should be considered during mechanical testing of tendons:
Variation of mechanical properties under nonphysiologic conditions
Inherent strength of tendon compared to testing instruments
Accurate measurement of cross-sectional area
Viscoelasticity of tendon
Proper storage of specimens
Importance of tendon orientation during testing

Biomechanics
Structural properties describe the overall load-bearing capacity of the tissue and include
the contribution of the muscle and bone attachments and the geometry of the tissue
(cross-sectional area and length). Structural properties include stiffness (the slope of the
linear portion of the curve shown in Figure 2 and failure load. Material properties (also
referred to as mechanical properties) describe the quality of the tissue. Material
properties are calculated by normalizing structural properties to account for tissue
geometry. Material properties include the modulus of elasticity (the slope of the linear
portion of the stress-strain curve) and failure stress (ie, strength).
Tendons from different anatomic locations have different structural properties; for
example, digital flexor tendons have twice the ultimate strength of digital extensor
tendons. The insertion of a tendon just distal to a joint allows for the tendon to act as a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
5/19

buttress against translation of the articular surfaces (eg, hamstring acting as a secondary
stabilizer for the anterior cruciate ligament [ACL]).1
Exercise has a positive effect and immobilization has a detrimental effect on the
biomechanical properties of tendons (Figure 3). The material and structural properties
of tendons increase from birth through maturity. The properties then decrease from
maturity through old age.
The mechanical properties of tendons vary with hydration, temperature, and pH;
therefore, tendons should be tested under physiologically relevant hydration,
temperature, and pH conditions. The high strength of tendons makes it difficult to grip
the tissue during mechanical testing. Specialized grips (eg, freeze clamps) often are
necessary to prevent the tendon from slipping out of the grip. Measurement of tissue
cross-sectional area is necessary for the calculation of stress (recall that stress =
load/cross-sectional area). Care must be taken in measuring the cross-sectional area of
tendon because the tissue will deform if contact methods (eg, calipers) are used.
Because tendons are viscoelastic (ie, their properties are time-dependent), the rate at
which the tendon is pulled may influence the mechanical properties. Higher strain rates
result in a higher elastic modulus. Specimens should be stored frozen and hydrated.
Improper storage may affect the mechanical properties of the tendon. The orientation of
a tendon during testing will influence the mechanical properties measured; for example,
the structural properties of the supraspinatus tendon depend on the angle of the
humeral head relative to the glenoid.

6/19

Figure 3 Graph shows that immobilization leads to a drastic drop in mechanical
properties and that exercise has a positive effect on mechanical properties. (Reproduced
with permission from Woo SL, Chan SS, Yamaji T: Biomechanics of knee ligament healing,
repair and reconstruction. J Biomech 1997;30[5]:431-439.)
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Tendon injury occurs because of direct trauma (eg, laceration of a flexor tendon) or indirect
tensile overload (eg, Achilles tendon rupture). Several tendinopathies (eg, rotator cuff
degeneration) predispose tendons to injury.
Three phases of healing
Hemostasis/inflammation
Cell proliferation and extracellular matrix production
Remodeling/maturation
Long-term effects—The structural properties of repaired tendons typically reach only two-
thirds of normal, even 1 year after repair. Material property differences are even higher.
Sheathed tendons—Flexor tendons of the hand often are injured via direct trauma (eg,
laceration). The two critical considerations for sheathed tendon healing are prevention of
adhesion formation and accrual of mechanical strength (Figure 4).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
7/19

Tendons not enclosed in sheaths fail because of trauma (eg, acute sports injury) or preexisting
pathology (eg, rotator cuff tear after years of chronic tendon degeneration). Nonsheathed
tendons have a greater capacity to heal than sheathed tendons. Injury often occurs at the
attachments of the tendon (ie, at the tendon-to-bone insertion or at the musculotendinous
junction).
The role of rehabilitation during healing is complex and may differ based on individual tendon
anatomy (ie, rotator cuff versus Achilles versus flexor tendons).
Fluoroquinolone antibiotic agents predispose patients to tendinopathy and have an adverse
effect on tendon healing after repair.
Figure 4 Illustration shows a sheathed tendon. Sheathed tendons heal primarily via infiltration of
fibroblasts from the outer and inner surfaces of the tendon (black arrow). Adhesions between the
outer surface of the tendon and the sheath (white arrows) can be prevented via passive motion
rehabilitation. (Image courtesy of Dr. R.H. Gelberman, Boston, MA.)

Injury, Repair, and Healing
After injury, the wound site is infiltrated by inflammatory cells. Immediately after injury,
erythrocytes and acute inflammatory cells, particularly neutrophils, enter the injury site.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
8/19

Within the first 24 hours postinjury, macrophages and monocytes infiltrate the injury
zone and begin phagocytosis of necrotic materials.2
During this time, platelets aggregate at the wound and create a fibrin clot to stabilize the
torn tendon edges. The length of this phase is on the order of days, typically lasting up to
1 week (Resource 2).3
During the late inflammatory phase, before revascularization of the tendon stumps, the
healing tendon is felt to be the weakest.4,5
During the proliferative phase that follows, beginning in the second week after injury,
fibroblasts infiltrate the injury site. They produce extracellular matrix, including large
amounts of type I and type III collagen. The injury response in adult tendon is scar
mediated (ie, large amounts of disorganized collagen are deposited at the repair site)
rather than regenerative. The length of this phase is on the order of several weeks. The
predominant growth factors present during this phase include transforming growth
factor-β, insulin-like growth factor 1, vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-derived
growth factor, and basic fibroblast growth factor.3 In rat models of rotator cuff tears,
tendon stiffness and collagen organization began to gradually increase after 2 weeks
postinjury.6
During the remodeling and maturation phase of healing that follows, matrix
metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade the collagen matrix, replacing type III collagen with
type I collagen. MMP-9 and MMP-13 participate primarily in collagen degradation,
whereas MMP-2, MMP-3, and MMP-14 participate in degradation and remodeling.3
Collagen fibers are reorganized so they are aligned in the direction of muscle loading.
The length of this phase is on the order of months to years. At 16 weeks postinjury in rat
models of supraspinatus tendon tears, which was the final time point observed, the
healing tendon continued to demonstrate increasing stiffness and collagen
organization.6
Protective immobilization in the early period after tendon repair may be beneficial in
many scenarios (eg, after rotator cuff repair). Active loading, including exercise, may be
detrimental if initiated too early in the rehabilitation period but is beneficial during the
remodeling phase of healing. Early passive motion is beneficial for flexor tendon healing.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
9/19

Early motion suppresses adhesion formation between the tendon and the sheath,
preventing the typical range-of-motion losses observed in immobilized tendons.
In rat models of supraspinatus tendon detachment and repair, shoulders that were
immobilized demonstrated improved structural, compositional, and quasilinear
viscoelastic properties compared with those that underwent early exercise.7 In rat
models of Achilles tendon tears, early exercise in the form of swimming did affect
functional or mechanical recovery of the ruptured Achilles tendon.8 In flexor tendon
injuries, canine forepaw models of flexor tendon repair demonstrated that early
controlled passive motion led to improved gliding function and improved ultimate tensile
load compared with immobilized tendons at 12 weeks.9
Administration of certain pharmacologic therapies, such as fluoroquinolone antibiotic
agents, has been shown to adversely affect tendon healing. In rat models of rotator cuff
repair, rats treated with the use of a fluoroquinolone antibiotic agent before and after
tendon tear and repair demonstrated much higher expression of certain MMPs, poorer
healing at the enthesis, and an increased risk of intrasubstance repair failure during
mechanical testing compared with control animals.10
Anatomic considerations of healing
Tendons may be intrasynovial, in which they are enclosed in a sheath that allows for
decreased friction, abrasion, and greater excursion, or extrasynovial.3
Tendon healing occurs intrinsically via proliferation of cells in the native tissue, such as
epitenon and endotenon tenocytes, or extrinsically via invasion of cells from the
surrounding tendon sheath or synovium. Although intrinsic healing is the goal of
management, extrinsic healing is the predominant mode of healing observed in tendon
ruptures seen clinically.3 Compared with extra-articular tendons and ligaments, intra-
articular tendons and ligaments tend to exhibit poor healing after tears. This may be
related to the intra-articular environment and, particularly, the failure of a fibrin clot to
form and serve as a provisional scaffold inside of joints.3

Ligaments
Function, Structure, and Composition
The function of ligaments is to restrict joint motion (ie, stabilize joints).
Composition and structure
Ligaments are composed of densely packed type I collagen, proteoglycans, elastin, and
water.
Ligaments are similar in composition and structure to tendons; however, several important
differences exist.
Ligaments are shorter and wider than tendons.
Ligaments have a lower percentage of collagen and a higher percentage of proteoglycans
and water.
The collagen fibers in ligaments are less organized.
Ligaments have a highly ordered hierarchical structure, similar to tendons.
Type I collagen contributes to approximately 70% of the dry weight of ligaments.
Similar to tendons, the main cell type in ligaments is the fibroblast; however, ligament
fibroblasts appear rounder than tendon fibroblasts.
Ligaments have relatively low vascularity and cellularity.
Biomechanical Properties
The biomechanical properties of ligaments are expressed as the structural properties of the
bone-ligament-bone complex or the material properties of the ligament midsubstance itself.
Ligaments exhibit viscoelastic behavior similar to that of tendons.
Several factors that influence the mechanical properties of ligaments are the same as those
described earlier for tendons.
Factors that must be considered in mechanically testing ligaments are the same as those listed
earlier for tendons.
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Ligament injuries generally are classified into three grades: I, II, and III. Grade I corresponds
with a mild sprain, grade II corresponds with a moderate sprain/partial tear, and grade III
corresponds with a complete ligament tear. An additional type of injury is avulsion of the
ligament from its bony insertion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
11/19

Ligament healing occurs via the same phases as tendon healing: hemostasis/inflammation,
matrix and cell proliferation, and remodeling/maturation.
Extra-articular ligaments (eg, the medial collateral ligament [MCL] of the knee) have a greater
capacity to heal than intra-articular ligaments (eg, the ACL of the knee). Notably, intra-articular
ligaments form an alpha-smooth muscle actin layer over the surfaces of ruptured ends that
leads to retraction and lack of bridging tissue at the repair site.3
MCL of the knee
Grade I and grade II injuries to the MCL heal without surgical management.
Optimal management of grade III MCL injuries is a subject of controversy. As many as 25%
of patients with these injuries continue to experience clinical problems regardless whether
the tear is repaired surgically.
ACL of the knee
Midsubstance ACL injuries typically do not heal. Surgical reconstruction of the ACL often is
necessary to restore stability in the injured knee. Several graft materials have been used to
reconstruct the ACL, including autografts and allografts.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
Autografts, including bone-patellar tendon-bone, semitendinosus and gracilis, and
quadriceps, are commonly used. The structural properties of the reconstructed graft
attain approximately 50% of normal ligament properties at the longest follow-up
studied. The major disadvantage of autografts is donor site morbidity. ACL allografts,
typically taken from cadaver models, also are used for ACL reconstruction.
Disadvantages of these grafts include the potential for disease transmission and the loss
of mechanical properties as a result of the graft sterilization processing. A process
described as ligamentization occurs in autografts and allografts after ACL reconstruction.
Animal studies suggest that autograft fibroblasts die soon after reconstruction and are
replaced by local fibroblasts. Similarly, allografts are infiltrated by local fibroblasts in the
early period after implantation. At the graft tendon and tunnel wall interface, a
transitional zone of vascularized, highly cellular granulation tissue is generated that

eventually leads to the formation of Sharpey-like fibers bridging tendon and bone.3 The
structure and composition of a native enthesis is not predictably reformed.
Enthesis
Structure, Function, and Composition
Tendons and ligaments insert into bone across a complex transitional tissue, the enthesis.
Composition and structure
Indirect insertions (eg, the femoral insertion of the MCL) have a superficial layer that
connects with the periosteum and a deep layer that anchors to bone via Sharpey fibers.
Direct insertions (eg, the supraspinatus insertion of the rotator cuff) classically have been
categorized into four zones:
First zone: tendon proper
Second zone: unmineralized fibrocartilage
Third zone: mineralized fibrocartilage
Fourth zone: bone
Although the insertion site typically is categorized into four zones, changes in the tissue are
graded, without distinct borders between zones (Figure 5). This graded transition in tissue
composition is presumed to aid in the efficient transfer of load between tendon and bone.

Figure 5 Bright field microscopic images (top row) and polarized light images (bottom row) show
canine flexor tendon-to-bone enthesis. Note that the transitional tissue between tendon and
bone is not regenerated at the healing interface. (Reproduced from Thomopoulos S: Tendons and
ligaments, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 656-662.)

Structure, Function, and Composition
The properties of the first zone (tendon proper) are similar to those found at the tendon
midsubstance. It consists of well-aligned type I collagen fibers with small amounts of the
proteoglycan decorin. The cell type in this zone is the fibroblast. The fibrocartilage zone
marks the beginning of the transition from tendinous material to bony material. It is
composed of type II and type III collagen, with small amounts of type I, type IX, and type
X collagen and small amounts of the proteoglycans aggrecan and decorin. The cell type
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:47 AM
AAOS | Tendons and Ligaments
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002110
14/19

in this zone is the fibrochondrocyte. The third zone consists of mineralized fibrocartilage.
This zone is characterized by a marked transition toward bony tissue. The predominant
collagen is type II, with considerable amounts of type X collagen and aggrecan. The cell
types in this zone are the fibrochondrocyte and the hypertrophic chondrocyte. The
fourth zone, bone, predominantly consists of type I collagen with a high mineral content.
The cell types in this zone are the osteoblast, osteocyte, and osteoclast.
Biomechanical Properties
A functionally graded transition between tendon and bone is necessary to reduce stress
concentrations at the interface of two different materials (tendon/ligament and bone).
Composition grading is evident in mineral content and proteoglycan content. Structural
grading is evident in collagen fiber organization. Mechanical grading is evident in elastic and
viscoelastic properties.
The enthesis typically has lower mechanical properties in tension than the tendon or ligament
midsubstance. This more compliant region between tendon/ligament and bone reduces stress
concentrations that would otherwise arise between the dissimilar materials and creates a
tough attachment.
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Tendon-to-bone and ligament-to-bone healing is necessary in several scenarios.
Rotator cuff injuries, which include most of the soft-tissue injuries to the upper extremity,
commonly require surgical repair of the tendon(s) to the humeral head.
Most ACL reconstruction techniques involve the use of tendon grafts that must heal in tibial
and femoral bone tunnels.
Avulsion injuries to the flexor tendons of the hand require tendon-to-bone repair.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
In most cases of tendon-to-bone healing, clinical outcomes are disappointing. The most
dramatic feature of the failed healing response is the lack of a transitional tissue
between the healing tendon and bone. Regeneration of the natural functionally graded

interface between tendon and bone is critical for the restoration of joint function and the
prevention of reinjury.
Tissue Engineering
Overview
Definition—Tissue engineering is the regeneration of injured tissue through the merging of
three areas: scaffold microenvironment, responding cells, and signaling biofactors.
Tissue engineering approaches hold great promise in improving tendon and ligament repair;
however, they have not yet succeeded clinically.
Scaffold microenvironment
The scaffold can serve as a delivery system for biofactors, an environment to attract or
immobilize cells, and/or a mechanical stabilizer.
Scaffold matrices commonly are made of collagen, fibrin, polymer, or silk.
Responding cells
Responding cells may include tendon/ligament fibroblasts or mesenchymal stromal cells
(commonly derived from bone marrow or adipose tissue).
Responding cells may be seeded onto the scaffold before implantation or may infiltrate the
acellular scaffold after it is implanted.
Signaling biofactors
Growth factors
Platelet-derived growth factor-BB promotes cell proliferation and matrix synthesis.
Transforming growth factor-β promotes matrix synthesis.
Basic fibroblast growth factor promotes cell proliferation and matrix synthesis.
Bone morphogenetic protein-12, -13, and -14 (also known as growth and differentiation
factors 7, 6, and 5, respectively) promote matrix synthesis and the differentiation of
mesenchymal stem cells into tendon/ligament fibroblasts.
Mechanical signals
Cyclic tensile loads promote matrix synthesis.
Compressive loads
Medical three-dimensional printing (Resource 3)
Traditional printing

Involves the creation of surgical models, surgical guides, orthotics, or permanent implants
with nonbiodegradable metals, plastics, or ceramics, or biodegradable polymers11
Advanced biomaterial printing
Involves the printing of acellular biomaterials that are fabricated from three- dimensional
printable inks to produce a tissue-specific response and desired regenerative behavior.11
Bioprinting
Bioprinting refers to the use of cell-encapsulating materials called bioinks, which are
composed of a matrix material (eg, a hydrogel) containing a type of living cell (eg, primary
cells, adult stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells).11
